terms.definition: An option on its final trading day, expiring at the end of the same session. Time decay and price swings are extremely compressed.
An option you can exercise at any point up to and including expiration.
The long-dated put in a poor man's covered put; shorter-term puts are sold against it again and again for income.
What happens to the option seller when the buyer exercises: the seller must fulfil the contract, buying or selling shares at the strike.
An option whose strike is at or very near the current price of the underlying.
The clearing house's practice of exercising expiring in-the-money options for the holder. The OCC's trigger is an option at least $0.01 in the money; your broker's rule may differ.
A spread with more long options than short, usually opened for a debit. It has large profit potential on one side.
A futures curve where later-dated contracts trade below nearer ones or below spot. Rolling into the cheaper contract can earn a gain.
In futures, the gap between the cash price of a commodity and its futures price. Elsewhere, basis can mean your cost for tax reporting.
One hundredth of one percent, used to describe small percentage differences.
A defined-risk credit spread: sell a call and buy a higher-strike call, profiting if the stock stays below the short strike. Also called a short call vertical.
A bearish debit spread: buy a higher-strike put and sell a lower-strike put, paying a net debit for a moderate decline.
How strongly a security's returns move with the market, which is set at 1.0. Higher means more market risk.
Converting all positions into one benchmark's terms, such as SPY deltas, so you can see how the whole portfolio reacts to a market move.
The gap between the best price a buyer offers and the best price a seller asks. A narrow gap signals a liquid option.
An iron condor with very wide spreads, approximating a short strangle while keeping risk defined. Neutral outlook, best in high IV.
terms.tasty_usage: Enters like a regular iron condor aiming for a credit of one third of the spread width; closes at a wider 25-50% of max profit; manages by rolling the untested side.

terms.definition: A long butterfly with very wide wings: more reward potential and more max loss, but lower probability. Neutral, defined risk, best in high IV.
terms.tasty_usage: Rarely traded; buys when volatility is very high, often financed by high-probability trades or turned into a broken wing; manages at 25-50% of max profit.

terms.definition: A rare, unpredictable event with severe and widespread market consequences, a term popularised by Nassim Taleb.
A closed-form formula that produces theoretical prices for European options.
The two middle-strike contracts of a butterfly, where maximum profit sits.
A butterfly with one wing wider than the other, which lets it be opened for a credit. Also called a skip-strike butterfly.
A defined-risk bullish debit spread: buy a lower-strike call and sell a higher-strike call.
A defined-risk credit spread: sell a put and buy a lower-strike put, profiting if the stock stays above the short strike. Also called a short put vertical.
Buying back an option you previously sold, ending your obligation.
The amount of account capital a position ties up while it is open.
Same strike and option type in two expirations, one bought and one sold. Profits from time decay differences and volatility changes.
terms.tasty_usage: Tends to buy calendars when IV is at extreme lows.

terms.definition: A vertical debit spread whose long leg expires later than the short leg.
A contract giving its buyer the right to buy 100 shares at the strike price any time up to expiration.
Settling an option or future by paying the cash difference rather than delivering the underlying. Cash-settled index options follow European exercise rules.
terms.tasty_usage: Prefers trading ETFs over cash-settled indexes, citing more efficient pricing, strike choice and volume.

terms.definition: A short put backed by enough cash to buy the shares if assigned.
Option that settles in cash based on strike versus underlying, with no asset delivery.
How an option's delta changes as time passes.
An iron condor collecting about half the strike width in credit instead of a third: bigger payout if right, smaller max loss if the stock overshoots. Common for earnings.
terms.tasty_usage: Typically used for earnings; closes at 50% of max profit, usually at the next morning's open; manages by rolling the untested side.

terms.definition: Owning shares, buying a protective put and selling an out-of-the-money call to help pay for it. Limits both downside and upside.
How an option's gamma changes as time passes.
The usual futures curve shape, with later contracts above spot or nearer contracts. Rolling VIX-linked products in contango bleeds value.
A statistic from -1 to +1 showing how closely two assets move together.
What you originally paid for a stock, including commissions and fees.
Lowering the effective price of shares by collecting option premium against them, such as selling covered calls. It limits upside but raises the chance of profit.
terms.tasty_usage: Reduces cost basis whenever possible, for example with monthly covered calls or by using spreads instead of naked long calls.

terms.definition: A collar where the credit from the short call roughly pays for the long put.
Owning 100 shares and selling one call against them, collecting income in exchange for capping upside.
A short option backed by owned shares or an offsetting option position.
A vertical spread where the sold option is worth more than the bought one, so you receive a net credit.
A notice that a pattern day trader account has fallen below its required minimum balance and needs funding.
A spread where the bought options cost more than the sold ones, so cash leaves your account up front.
terms.tasty_usage: Prefers debit spreads over credit spreads for directional trades in low IV.

terms.definition: The expected change in an option's price for a $1 move in the underlying; also used as a rough measure of directional exposure.
A position whose net delta is near zero, so small price moves barely change its value. Isolates volatility edge from direction.
A security whose price depends on an underlying asset, such as options and futures.
Options of the same type at different strikes and different expirations, one long and one short.
Annual dividends per share divided by the current share price.
A Do Not Exercise instruction to your broker for a long in-the-money option you want to let expire.
The long-run underperformance of funds that rebalance daily, such as VXX, because futures in contango are sold for less than the next contract costs.
Number of days until an option expires. Also called duration; sets how much time decay and time to be right.
terms.tasty_usage: Targets 25-50 DTE at entry, with 45 days the sweet spot; duration is the first thing to change when managing.

terms.definition: A company's periodic public report of results, usually quarterly and quoted as earnings per share.
Net profit attributable to common shares divided by shares outstanding.
The gap between a company's actual results and analyst expectations.
Implied volatility inflated by an earnings release. It peaks just before the announcement and collapses right after.
terms.tasty_usage: Sells premium into earnings and closes at the open after the announcement.

terms.definition: Unsecured debt issued by a bank that tracks a benchmark and trades like a stock; it owns none of the underlying assets.
An option that can be exercised only at expiration.
The risk of sudden large moves from unforeseeable occurrences, including binary outcomes.
The first day a stock trades without the right to the upcoming dividend. Buy before it to receive the payout.
The one-standard-deviation range a stock is expected to trade in, derived from its price, implied volatility and days to expiration.
terms.tasty_usage: For binary events such as earnings, estimates it as 85% of the front-month ATM straddle price.

terms.definition: The date an option stops trading, after which it is exercised or becomes worthless.
The part of an option's price above intrinsic value, reflecting time and implied volatility. Also called time value; it decays to zero by expiration.
A company's own projections of its future performance.
Differences in implied volatility across expiration dates, also called term structure skew.
The nearest regular monthly expiration, also called near or spot month.
A vertical spread with an extra short option at the short strike, opened for a net credit.
An option giving the right, not the obligation, to enter a specific futures contract at a set strike. Futures gains and losses are settled daily.
How fast an option's delta changes for each $1 move in the underlying.
Repeatedly adjusting stock hedges to keep a position delta-neutral as delta drifts.
An order that stays active until it fills, expires or you cancel it.
A position taken to offset or reduce risk in another position or the portfolio.
The number of shares needed to offset an options position's delta: contracts times delta times the multiplier.
Trades used when implied volatility is high, such as strangles, iron condors, verticals, covered calls and naked puts, aiming to profit from volatility falling back.
terms.tasty_usage: Sells premium when IV is high; for binary events uses tasty strategies like the beef n' cheddar or super bull.

terms.definition: A hedge whose price moves do not fully offset the risk it targets.
The market's expected annualised one-standard-deviation move in the underlying, backed out of option prices.
terms.tasty_usage: Looks at IV rank rather than raw IV for context; sells premium when IV is high and may buy debit or calendar spreads when low.

terms.definition: How far an option is in the money; zero if out of the money.
Selling puts above calls (or calls below puts) in a short position, usually the result of adjustments after a big move rather than an opening setup.
terms.tasty_usage: Avoids opening inverted trades; uses inversion only if necessary to reduce a loss or break even.

terms.definition: A bull put spread and bear call spread sharing the same short strike. Pays more credit than an iron condor but has a narrower profit range.
A neutral, defined-risk trade combining a short put spread and a short call spread, profiting if the stock stays between the short strikes.
terms.tasty_usage: Aims to collect about a third of the strike width in credit and closes at 50% of max profit.

terms.definition: An option with intrinsic value: a call whose strike is below the stock price, or a put whose strike is above it.
A sharp drop in implied volatility, typically right after an anticipated event like earnings resolves.
Implied volatility reverting toward its average: high IV tends to contract, low IV tends to expand. Option prices rise and fall with it.
terms.tasty_usage: Bases trades on IV mean reversion, using IV rank to choose credit or debit strategies.

terms.definition: The share of days in the past year when implied volatility was below today's level.
Where current implied volatility sits between its 52-week low and high, on a 0 to 100 scale.
terms.tasty_usage: Prefers IV rank over raw IV when deciding to sell or buy premium.

terms.definition: A short put combined with a short call spread for a net credit, with no upside risk when credit exceeds the call spread width.
The percentage change in an option's price per 1% move in the underlying; a measure of leverage.
Long-dated options, with expirations a year or more out, up to two or three years.
One component of a multi-part position, such as the call or put in a straddle.
Opening or closing each leg of a spread in separate transactions rather than as one order. It can improve fills but adds risk.
terms.tasty_usage: Tries to avoid legging in and out; may leg out to exit quickly, such as after earnings.

terms.definition: Using a small amount of capital to control a large amount of securities.
The value of underlying exposure divided by the capital spent on the option.
Funds that amplify an underlying's daily move by a multiplier, some inversely. Daily rebalancing causes long-term drag.
terms.tasty_usage: Avoids them long term, using them only for short-term speculation.

terms.definition: Capping potential profit, for example with spreads or covered calls, in exchange for a higher probability of success.
terms.tasty_usage: Deliberately limits profit to raise probability of profit, and trades small.

terms.definition: The risk of having to accept a poor price because you cannot sell quickly.
Buying futures to lock in a purchase price for an asset you plan to buy.
Buying a call and a put at the same strike and expiration to profit from a large move in either direction.
Trades used when implied volatility is low: calendars, debit spreads and other plays that benefit from volatility expanding.
terms.tasty_usage: Still hunts for high-IV underlyings, since premium selling is the main edge.

terms.definition: Closing a trade before expiration and before reaching max profit.
terms.tasty_usage: Manages at a set percent of max profit, a mechanical closing point.

terms.definition: The capital a broker requires you to hold to open and carry a trade. Portfolio margin reflects actual account risk instead of fixed percentages.
A broker demand for more funds when account equity falls below the required level.
Valuing a position at its current market price; futures gains and losses are credited or debited to the account daily.
Your hypothesis about how an asset or market will behave, which determines the trade you choose.
An order that fills immediately at current prices when counterparties exist, trading price certainty for execution certainty.
100 short shares plus a long out-of-the-money call for protection.
100 shares plus a long put to define downside, acting like a stop loss.
The tendency of prices or volatility to drift back toward a long-term average. Volatility is the most reliable example.
terms.tasty_usage: Is a contrarian mean-reversion trader: rolls losers while the assumption holds and sells into strength.

terms.definition: Whether an option is in, at or out of the money, based on strike versus the underlying price.
A short option not hedged by shares or an offsetting option.
An asset that tends to move opposite to the market, useful for hedging or diversification.
Two assets tending to move in opposite directions; coefficient between -1 and 0.
Short-option exposure where delta moves against the seller as price moves.
A volatility skew where out-of-the-money puts carry higher implied volatility than at- or in-the-money options.
The total value of the underlying a position controls, regardless of the amount paid to open it.
How many repeated trades are needed for realized results to approach the true odds. More small trades make outcomes more reliable.
The total number of outstanding option contracts not yet closed, exercised or expired.
The price paid by the buyer and received by the seller of an option.
The clearing house that guarantees options contracts and randomly assigns exercise notices to sellers.
The number of shares one contract controls, normally 100 for equity options.
An option with no intrinsic value.
Trading a temporary breakdown in the relationship between two correlated underlyings, such as selling the one that rose and buying the one that lagged.
terms.tasty_usage: Checks that correlations have not detached before trading a pair.

terms.definition: A margin account holder who makes four or more day trades in a rolling five-day period, and must keep a $25,000 minimum balance.
terms.tasty_usage: tastylive's page predates the change: FINRA replaced the PDT rule and its $25,000 minimum with intraday margin standards effective 2026-06-04 [lit:finra-rn26-10-2026].

terms.definition: A correlation coefficient of exactly +1.
Settlement where the underlying asset is actually transferred on exercise.
The risk that the stock closes right at your strike at expiration, making assignment uncertain and possibly leaving unwanted exposure after expiration.
A long call diagonal that replaces the shares in a covered call with a long-dated call, paired with a short near-term call.
A long-dated put used instead of short stock, paired with near-term short puts for income.
The estimated chance a trade makes at least $0.01. For a credit spread, roughly one minus credit divided by width.
terms.tasty_usage: Entry POP above 50%; closer to 50% pays more credit, closer to 100% pays less.

terms.definition: Two assets tending to move together; coefficient between 0 and +1.
Long-option exposure where delta moves in the holder's favour as price moves.
A reverse skew in which out-of-the-money calls carry higher implied volatility than other options.
A position that gains value as time passes, typical of short options.
A position that gains when implied volatility rises, as with owned options.
The relationship between expected reward and risk. Good pot odds mean risking less than you stand to make.
terms.tasty_usage: Alters pot odds in its favour through IV reversion, rolling and managing winners.

terms.definition: A put bought against owned shares to set a floor on the sale price.
A contract giving its buyer the right to sell 100 shares at the strike price by expiration.
The pricing link between a call, a put with the same strike and expiry, and the stock.
How much an underlying actually moved over a past period, also called historical volatility.
Re-adjusting a hedge as delta drifts.
Max potential profit on a short position divided by the capital it uses. Puts different trades on one scale.
terms.tasty_usage: Weighs ROC against POP to use capital efficiently.

terms.definition: A net-debit long version made of a long put spread and a long call spread, profiting from a big move either way.
An option's sensitivity to a 1% change in interest rates.
Closing an existing option and opening a new one, changing strike, expiration or both.
terms.tasty_usage: Rolls defensively for duration, only if the assumption is unchanged, ideally for a credit; does not double size.

terms.definition: Gain from rolling an expiring futures position into a cheaper later contract in backwardation.
Adjusting trade size and structure as the account grows or shrinks, for instance by widening spreads rather than adding contracts.
terms.tasty_usage: Scales by widening wings, adding positions and going further OTM; scales down after a bad run.

terms.definition: Buying and selling the same underlying several times in one day for small gains. Needs high liquidity.
A non-equity option category taxed on a blended 60/40 long-term and short-term basis.
Selling options to collect premium, aiming to profit from time decay and a drop in implied volatility. Gains in three price scenarios, versus one for buyers.
terms.tasty_usage: Primary strategy, selling in high IV to keep portfolio theta positive.

terms.definition: A sold call that obliges the seller to deliver shares at the strike if exercised. Risk is unlimited.
Selling futures to lock in a sale price for an asset you own.
Selling a call and a put at the same strike and expiration to profit from stable prices and time decay.
An iron condor with unequal wing widths or strikes, adding a directional lean by shifting risk to one side.
terms.tasty_usage: Used in high IV or when it has a directional bias.

terms.definition: One-time payout outside the regular schedule, often from surplus cash.
How an option's gamma changes as the underlying price changes.
The current price for immediate delivery.
A measure of how widely outcomes spread around an average; for options it is tied to implied volatility ranges.
Placing many small high-probability trades to avoid drawdowns that are hard to recover from.
terms.tasty_usage: Trades small and often to build more occurrences.

terms.definition: Using a deep in-the-money long call instead of shares for leverage.
A conditional order that becomes a market order once the stock trades at the stop price.
A call and a put with different out-of-the-money strikes in the same expiration.
The fixed price at which an option holder may buy (call) or sell (put) the underlying.
A bullish earnings trade: buy a call spread and sell a far out-of-the-money naked call to finance it, shifting risk from downside to upside.
terms.tasty_usage: Used mainly for earnings with a strong bullish view; the short call strike is chosen far OTM.

terms.definition: A position built from different instruments to mimic another, such as a long call plus short put imitating long stock.
terms.tasty_usage: Uses synthetics to take part in products otherwise too big for a small account.

terms.definition: Market-wide risk that diversification cannot remove.
The side of a short strangle the stock is threatening; the other side is untested.
The expected daily change in an option's value from time passing.
The steady erosion of an option's extrinsic value as expiration nears.
Instruction for how long an order stays working before being cancelled, e.g. day, GTC, IOC or FOK.
A stop whose trigger follows the market at a fixed percent or point distance.
A neutral, undefined-risk trade selling an OTM call and an OTM put spread; the reverse of a jade lizard, rarely suited because skew usually favours puts.
terms.tasty_usage: Finds it underperforms jade lizards; best used when skew inverts.

terms.definition: How vomma changes as implied volatility changes, a third-order volatility sensitivity.
A position, like a naked call, whose max loss is unknown at entry. Brokers set margin from a roughly two-standard-deviation move.
Risk specific to one company, sector or asset that diversification can reduce.
A leveraged product targeting twice the daily return of a short-term VIX futures index, with strong decay.
The randomness of small samples of results around expectation.
An option's price sensitivity to a 1 point change in implied volatility.
Two options of the same type and expiration at different strikes, one long and one short.
An index of expected 30-day S&P 500 volatility, derived from option prices, known as the fear gauge.
The idea that VIX moves hint at future market conditions.
terms.tasty_usage: Uses VIX movement to gauge what kind of market lies ahead.

terms.definition: The size of fluctuations in a security's price, expressed as annualised standard deviation of returns.
Instruments for trading volatility directly, such as VIX options and futures, VXX, UVXY and SVXY. Contango makes holding them long term costly.
Variation in implied volatility across strikes and expirations of the same underlying.
Number of contracts traded in a period.
How an option's vega changes as implied volatility changes.
The ticker for VIX futures, which settle in cash. Priced on expected future volatility, and exposed to carry costs from contango.
terms.tasty_usage: Uses /VX to trade low-volatility extremes or hedge; exits or rolls before expiry to avoid settlement risk.

terms.definition: An exchange-traded note tracking a blend of the front two VIX futures. Contango erodes its value over time.
A loss disallowed when the same or a substantially identical security is bought within 30 days before or after the sale.
Options with weekly expiration cycles. They are less liquid and hold less theta than monthlies.
terms.tasty_usage: Avoids weeklys except for earnings plays.

terms.definition: The outer long options of a butterfly or iron condor, capping risk.
Selling an option to open; the seller is the writer.
Zero extrinsic value back ratio: two ITM longs against one ATM short, giving a near-100-delta stock replacement.
How an option's gamma changes as implied volatility changes.
